parts.title: The bridge in my town
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
My father is an engineer, and he builds bridges. When I was small, I thought this was the best job in the world, and I still think so. Our town has one very old bridge across the river, and he says that it is the most beautiful one in the country.

The bridge is made of grey stone and has five arches. It was built more than two hundred years ago, without any machines, by workers who carried every stone by hand. Every year, thousands of tourists come to take photographs of it, and in summer, children jump into the river from its low wall, although this is not allowed.

Last winter, there was a very big flood, and the river rose almost to the top of the arches. Everyone in the town was afraid that the bridge would fall. My father and his team worked day and night to check it, and in the end, it survived without a single crack.

When I told my teacher about this, she asked me to write about it for school. I wrote that old bridges are like old people: they have seen many things, and they are stronger than they look.

questions.prompt: What does the writer think about her father's job?
options: It is the best job in the world
It is too difficult for most people
It is easier than it looks
It takes him away from the family
questions.explanation: She thought, and still thinks, that it is the best job in the world.

questions.prompt: How was the bridge built?
options: Using stones from the old castle
By a team of foreign engineers
With the help of big machines
By workers who carried the stones
questions.explanation: Workers carried every stone by hand, without any machines.

questions.prompt: What do some children do in the summer?
options: They jump from the bridge wall
questions.explanation: Children jump into the river from its low wall.

questions.prompt: What happened to the bridge during the flood?
options: It lost one of its arches
It was closed for a long time
It was not damaged at all
The river water went over it
questions.explanation: It survived without a single crack.

questions.prompt: What did the writer say in her school work?
options: Old bridges are stronger than they look
Rivers should never be built on
Floods are a great danger to towns
questions.explanation: She wrote that old bridges are stronger than they look.

parts.title: The race to the sky
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
For hundreds of years, the tallest buildings in the world were churches and towers. Then, at the end of the nineteenth century, a new kind of building appeared in the United States: the skyscraper. [1] Two things made this possible: steel and the lift.

Steel is much stronger than stone, so builders could make walls that were thinner and higher. [2] Before that invention, nobody wanted to live or work on the tenth floor, because the stairs were too tiring.

Soon, cities around the world began to compete. [3] Each new tower was taller than the last, and people loved to watch the cranes lift the steel high above the streets.

Today, the tallest skyscraper is more than eight hundred metres high. [4] It has more than a hundred and sixty floors, and the lift to the top takes about a minute.

Of course, tall buildings use a lot of energy. [5] Because of this, many architects now design towers with plants on the walls and solar panels on the roof.
sentences: The first examples were only about ten floors high.
This has become a serious worry for the planet.
They were popular with tourists from the very beginning.
Some towers sway a little in strong winds, but they are safe.
The lift was just as important, because it carried people up quickly.
Paris, London and Dubai all wanted the highest tower.
People who live in cold climates prefer small houses.
It is so tall that, on a clear day, it can be seen from a hundred kilometres away.

gaps.explanation: The first examples were only ten floors high, which follows the arrival of the skyscraper and leads to steel and the lift.
The lift carried people up quickly, and the next sentence says nobody wanted to live on the tenth floor before.
Paris, London and Dubai wanted the highest tower, which describes cities competing.
The sentence about being seen from a hundred kilometres away describes the very tall skyscraper.
The worry for the planet follows the energy use, and the next sentence says architects now use plants and solar panels.

parts.title: Why bridges stay up
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: A bridge has to carry a very heavy load. Think of all the cars, lorries and people [1] cross it every day! To do this, engineers use a few clever ideas. The first one is the arch: in an old stone bridge, the weight is pushed to the sides and down [2] the ground. Modern bridges often hang from strong steel cables, which are like giant ropes. These cables are attached to tall towers, [3] hold most of the weight. Engineers also test every bridge with computers before they begin to build it. They want to be sure [4] it can survive strong winds and floods. A good bridge can stay in place for a hundred years or [5], and it only needs a little care. When you cross a bridge, [6] a moment to think about the people who designed it.

gaps.explanation: People who cross it: a relative pronoun for people.
The weight goes down into the ground at the sides.
Towers which hold most of the weight: a relative pronoun.
Be sure that it can survive: a clause after sure.
A hundred years or more means longer than a hundred years.
Take a moment to think: a common phrase.

parts.instructions: Listen to seven short conversations. Choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Good afternoon, and thank you for coming to this meeting about the new tower by the harbour. First, a few facts. The old water tower, which will come down in March, is about a hundred metres high. The architects first drew a tower of four hundred metres, which would have been the tallest in the country, but the airport said no, because planes fly nearby, and the cost was enormous. So the council chose a smaller version. It will be exactly two hundred metres tall, with a restaurant at the top and a viewing platform for visitors. Building starts in the autumn. Now, I’ll take your questions.

question.prompt: How high will the new tower be?
question.explanation: The old tower is a hundred metres and the first plan of four hundred was refused; the final tower will be two hundred metres.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Are you coming to the castle tomorrow, Emeric?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I’ve been there already. Be ready for a long climb. There are three hundred steps to the top, and I counted every one of them.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I read that the lift is out of order.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: It was last week, but they’ve repaired it. I took it on the way down, and it’s very slow.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: And what about the weather? The forecast says cloudy.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: It said that for me too, but the sky was clear and the view was amazing.

turns.speaker: f

question.prompt: What does the man warn the woman about at the castle?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Good morning, here is your travel news. The old bridge in Riverton is closed to all traffic. Early this morning there was a rumour of an accident, but the police say that nobody was hurt and there was no crash. Workers will paint the bridge next month, but that has not started yet. The real reason is the weather: the wind is so strong, with gusts of eighty kilometres an hour, that it’s not safe for lorries or buses. Drivers should use the south road or the ferry, and allow an extra twenty minutes. We will tell you as soon as the bridge reopens.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Why do you always look for old flats, Enzo? New ones have lifts and everything.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: They aren’t cheaper to rent, you know. Old flats in the centre are usually more expensive. And they’re really hard to find, I’ve been looking for months.

turns.speaker: f

turns.speaker: m

turns.speaker: f

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Fair enough.

question.explanation: Old flats are expensive and hard to find; he likes them because each has a story, like the message under the paint.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: You visited the new library, didn’t you? What did you think?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Some things were great. The size surprised me. I expected it to be small because it looks narrow from outside, but inside it’s huge. And the glass roof is lovely, you can read in the sunlight.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Sounds perfect.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Almost. The chairs, though! They’re beautiful but really hard, after an hour my back hurt. I’d bring a cushion.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I’ll take one then.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Hi Tom, it’s Ruth. You asked when the new museum opens. The sign by the gate says summer, but that sign is old. First they said autumn, last year, you remember. Then there was a leak in the roof, and they moved the date to the summer. But I read in the paper yesterday that it will open in spring now, because the builders worked faster than they expected. The dinosaur room will be ready too, and I know your sister wants to see it. Let’s go together in April. Call me when you can. Bye.

question.explanation: The sign says summer and the first date was autumn, but both are old; the newspaper says it will open in spring.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Have you chosen your university course, Elara?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Yes, I send the form tomorrow. I nearly chose art history, because I love museums, but my mum says there are no jobs. And my dad wants me to study engineering, because I’m good at maths. He says I could build roads and bridges.

turns.speaker: m

turns.speaker: m

turns.text: I’m very happy, I’ve wanted a garden since I was little. I’ll plant tomatoes and herbs.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I hear you’re going to build your own house, Dan. Is it cheaper?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Not at all. It will probably cost more than buying one. And it’s not about my parents, they live two hours away anyway, and I’m not moving next to them.

turns.speaker: f

parts.title: A talk about the Golden Gate Bridge
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: bernice
turns.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I would like to tell you about one of the most famous bridges in the world, the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco. Let’s begin with the dates. Work started in nineteen thirty-three, and many people thought the project was impossible. It opened to the public in nineteen thirty-seven, in the month of May. Some books say nineteen thirty-six, but that is when the last part was joined; the opening party was a year later. So, how long did it take? The builders worked for four years, although the plans took even longer, more than ten years of discussions. Now, size. The bridge is long, nearly three kilometres, but what impresses visitors most are the two towers. They are more than two hundred metres high, and when the bridge opened they were the tallest in the world. The cables are even thicker than you imagine, about a metre across. People often ask me about the name. It is called Golden, but it isn’t gold at all. Its colour is a kind of orange-red. Engineers chose it because it looks good against the green hills and the blue sea. The navy wanted black and yellow stripes, but the engineers refused. Another reason for this colour is that it is easy to see in the fog, which covers the bridge on many days, especially in summer. Rain is rare, but fog is common, and ships can see the towers even when the visibility is poor. Finally, let me give you some advice for your visit. Many people go in the afternoon, but the wind is very strong then and the car park is full. Some prefer the evening for the sunset, but it can be cold. I recommend the morning, when it’s quiet, and the light is soft for photographs. Walk across the bridge, it takes about an hour, and bring a warm jacket. Thank you, and enjoy your day.

gaps.prompt: The opening party took place in the year nineteen thirty-___
gaps.explanation: Some books say nineteen thirty-six, but the opening party was a year later, in thirty-seven.
The plans took more than ten years, but the builders worked for four years.

gaps.prompt: Each of the two towers is taller than ___ metres
gaps.explanation: The bridge is nearly three kilometres long, but the towers are more than two hundred metres high.

gaps.prompt: The paint is a shade between orange and ___
gaps.explanation: It is not gold and the navy wanted black and yellow, but the colour is orange-red.

gaps.prompt: The colour helps ships to see the towers when there is ___
gaps.explanation: Rain is rare; the colour is easy to see in the fog.

gaps.prompt: The best part of the day for visitors is the ___
gaps.explanation: The afternoon is windy and the evening is cold, so she recommends the morning.

parts.title: An interview with an architect
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Emeric, you’re an architect. When did you first become interested in buildings?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Very early. When I was ten, my parents took me to see a famous bridge, and everybody was amazed, but honestly I was bored, I only wanted an ice cream. A school project was different: our teacher asked us to draw a plan of the school, and I got a bad mark, ha! But that same year I built a model of our house from cardboard, with every room and a tiny garden. I spent two weeks on it, and it’s still in my mother’s attic.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What does your day look like? Is it mostly drawing?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: People imagine that, but I draw perhaps two hours a day. Teaching? I tried it at a night school for a year, and I didn’t continue. And I don’t sell land, that’s a different profession. Most of my day I’m talking: to clients about what they want, and to the builders about how to do it. A house is a conversation between many people.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Why do you say that a building must be useful before anything else?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: It’s important that it looks beautiful, but to me that comes second. If a building is cheap, that’s good for the owner, but not the first thing. First, it must be useful, because people spend most of their lives inside buildings. A school with dark classrooms is a bad school, however pretty its walls are.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do you find hardest in your work?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: The computers are a pain, a new program every year, but I enjoy learning. Finding clients was hard when I began, now they come to me. The difficult part is money. Clients want more rooms and a lower price, and I have to say no to them. I hate that.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: You designed a village school. Why are you proud of it?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: It didn’t win any prize, and it’s not very tall, just one floor. But the children helped, and that’s what I love. They painted the walls in the corridor with their hands, and now the building belongs to them. When I visit, they show me their favourite corner.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Finally, what do you advise young people who want to follow your career?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Don’t think you must study maths all day, though you need some. And you needn’t travel to famous cities at first. Just look carefully at the buildings around you: your street, your school, the bus station. Ask yourself why it’s built that way. That’s how I learned.

He drew a plan of his school

questions.prompt: What does he advise young people to do?
options: Look carefully at the buildings around them
questions.explanation: He says maths all day and famous cities are not needed; he tells them to look carefully at nearby buildings.

parts.title: Getting to know you
parts.instructions: Answer each question in your own words. Aim to speak for 20-30 seconds.

questions.prompt: Do you live in a house or a flat? What is it like?
What is the most interesting building in your town?
Do you like heights? Why or why not?
What do you like to build or make?

parts.title: Describe a photograph
parts.instructions: Look at the photograph and speak for about one minute. Describe what you can see and say what the people might be feeling.
parts.prompt: A group of tourists on a viewing platform at the top of a tower.

parts.title: A visit to a famous building
parts.instructions: Look at the pictures. Talk about the options and decide which one is best.
parts.prompt: Your class is going on a trip to see famous buildings. Talk about the different places that you could visit and decide which one would be the most interesting.

parts.title: Talk about the topic
parts.instructions: Answer the questions. Try to give a reason or an example with each answer.

questions.prompt: Do you prefer old buildings or new ones? Why?
What makes a building beautiful, in your opinion?
Would you like to be an architect or an engineer? Why or why not?
